title: Greedy Algorithms
html:
A greedy algorithm builds a solution one piece at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now and never revisiting it. When the problem has the right structure this is the fastest possible approach; when it does not, greedy quietly returns a wrong answer.

Greedy algorithm — an algorithm that makes the locally optimal choice at every step, hoping (or proving) that these local choices add up to a globally optimal solution. There is no backtracking and no look-ahead — a choice once made is final.

Minimum coins — the motivating example

You have an infinite supply of coins of value 10, 5, 2, 1. Someone asks for an amount — how do you pay it with the fewest coins? The natural instinct is greedy: hand over the largest coin that still fits, repeat.

Example

Input: coins = [10, 5, 2, 1], amount = 52
Output: 6 (10 10 10 10 10 2)
Input: coins = [10, 5, 2, 1], amount = 93
Output: 11 (10 ×9, 2, 1)

Idea

Sort the denominations in decreasing order. For each denomination take as many coins as still fit (amount // coin), subtract them and move to the next smaller coin. The amount shrinks fastest when the biggest coin is used first.

Time O(k log k) to sort k denominations, then O(k)Space O(1) extra
Key point

This works for 10, 5, 2, 1 (and for every real currency system) because each coin is at least double the next smaller one, so a larger coin never has to be replaced by several smaller ones. That is a property of the input, not of greedy in general — see the counterexample below.

General structure of a greedy algorithm

Every greedy algorithm has the same skeleton: order the candidates by some selection rule, then scan them once, keeping each candidate that keeps the partial solution feasible.

1
Define the selection rule
What makes one candidate look better than another? Largest value, earliest finish, highest value-per-weight… This is the whole design — pick it wrong and the algorithm is wrong.
2
Sort (or use a heap)
Usually the candidates are sorted once by the rule, costing O(n log n); Huffman and Dijkstra instead pull the current best from a priority queue.
3
Scan once
Walk the candidates in order; accept each one that is still feasible, skip the rest. No step is ever undone.
4
Prove it
Argue that the greedy choice is always part of some optimal solution. Without this step you only have a heuristic.

When greedy works — and when it fails

A greedy algorithm is correct only when the problem has two properties:

Greedy-choice property

A globally optimal solution can be reached by making the locally optimal choice first — the first greedy pick is never a mistake. Proved by an exchange argument: take any optimal solution that does not contain the greedy choice, swap the greedy choice in, and show the result is no worse.

Optimal substructure

After the greedy choice is made, what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem, and an optimal solution to the whole is the greedy choice plus an optimal solution to the remainder.

Change the coin system and the greedy-choice property disappears. With coins 18, 10, 1 and amount 20, greedy grabs 18 first and is then forced to add two 1s — three coins — while the optimum is 10 + 10.

Pitfall

Greedy looks right on a few hand-made examples far more often than it is right. If you cannot state why the greedy choice is safe (an exchange argument), assume it is not and reach for dynamic programming — the 0/1 knapsack, general coin change and longest common subsequence are all problems where greedy fails.

Where greedy is used

Greedy shines in two situations: problems with a provable greedy-choice property, where it gives the fastest exact algorithm, and hard problems where a fast approximate answer is good enough.

Activity selection

Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals — earliest finish first. Solved below.

Fractional knapsack

Fill a bag of limited capacity with divisible items — highest value per weight first. Solved below.

Job sequencing

Schedule unit-time jobs with deadlines for maximum profit — highest profit first. Solved below.

Huffman coding

Build an optimal prefix code — repeatedly merge the two rarest symbols. Solved below.

Prim's & Kruskal's

Minimum spanning tree — always add the cheapest safe edge (see Graphs).

Dijkstra's algorithm

Shortest paths — always settle the closest unsettled vertex (see Graphs).

Approximation

For NP-hard problems such as the Travelling Salesman Problem, greedy heuristics (nearest-neighbour, cheapest insertion) are used to get a reasonably good tour quickly, even though they do not guarantee the optimum.

Activity selection problem

Given n activities with start and finish times, find the maximum number of activities a single person (or single-tasking machine) can perform — two activities can both be chosen only if they do not overlap.

Example

Input: activities = [(2, 3), (1, 4), (5, 8), (6, 10)] as (start, finish)
Output: 2 → (2, 3) and (5, 8)

Idea

Always pick the activity that finishes earliest — it frees the machine as soon as possible and leaves the most room for the rest. Picking by shortest duration or earliest start both fail on simple counterexamples.

1
Sort by finish time
Ascending — the activity ending first comes first.
2
Take the first activity
It is always part of some optimal solution (exchange argument: any optimal solution's first activity can be swapped for this one without creating an overlap).
3
Scan the rest
If the current activity starts at or after the finish of the last chosen one, choose it; otherwise it overlaps — skip it.
Time O(n log n) for the sort; O(n) if already sortedSpace O(1) extra
Key point

Why earliest finish is safe (exchange argument). Let S be any optimal set of activities and let g be the activity that finishes first overall. Replace the first activity of S with g: g finishes no later, so it cannot overlap the second activity of S. The new set is still valid and has the same size — so an optimal solution containing the greedy choice always exists.

Pitfall

Use start >= last_finish, not >. An activity may begin at the very instant the previous one ends; writing > throws away valid pairs like (1, 3) and (3, 5).

Fractional knapsack problem

A knapsack can carry at most W units of weight. Each item has a weight and a value, and — unlike the 0/1 knapsack — you may take any fraction of an item. Maximise the total value carried.

Example

Input: weights = [50, 20, 30], values = [600, 500, 400], W = 70
Output: 1140.00

Idea

Value per unit weight is what matters. Sort the items by value / weight descending, take whole items while they fit, then fill the remaining capacity with a fraction of the next item and stop — the knapsack is full.

Item (w, v)Ratio v/wDecisionValue addedCapacity left
(20, 500)25.0take all50050
(30, 400)13.3take all40020
(50, 600)12.0take 20/50600 × 20/50 = 2400
Time O(n log n)Space O(1) extra (O(n) if the input must not be reordered)
Pitfall

The ratio rule is only correct because items are divisible. In the 0/1 knapsack (take an item whole or not at all) the same greedy fails: with W = 50 and items (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120) the ratio order gives 160, but 100 + 120 = 220 is optimal. 0/1 knapsack needs dynamic programming.

Job sequencing problem

Each job has a deadline and a profit, takes exactly one unit of time, and only one job can run at a time starting from time 0. A job earns its profit only if it finishes by its deadline. Which jobs should be scheduled, and when, to maximise total profit?

Example

Input: jobs = a(2, 100) b(1, 19) c(2, 27) d(1, 25) e(3, 15) as (deadline, profit), slots = 3
Output: 142 → slot 1: c, slot 2: a, slot 3: e

Idea

Consider jobs in decreasing order of profit. Give each job the latest free slot that is still before its deadline — leaving the earlier slots open for jobs with tighter deadlines that come later in the scan.

1
Sort by profit, descending
a(100), c(27), d(25), b(19), e(15).
2
a (deadline 2)
Latest free slot ≤ 2 is slot 2 → schedule a there.
3
c (deadline 2)
Slot 2 is taken, slot 1 is free → schedule c in slot 1.
4
d (deadline 1), b (deadline 1)
Slot 1 is taken → both are dropped.
5
e (deadline 3)
Slot 3 is free → schedule e. Total profit 100 + 27 + 15 = 142.
Time O(n log n + n · slots) — O(n log n) with a disjoint-set to find the latest free slotSpace O(slots)
Pitfall

Placing a job in the earliest free slot instead of the latest one is the common mistake: a would take slot 1, and then c (deadline 2) still fits in slot 2 here, but in general early slots are the scarce resource that tight-deadline jobs need. Scanning backwards from min(slots, deadline) keeps them free.

Huffman coding

Huffman coding is a lossless compression scheme that gives each character a variable-length binary code: frequent characters get short codes, rare ones get long codes. Over the text "aabbacbababbabbabaab…" of 100 characters with frequencies a: 70, b: 20, c: 10, a fixed-length code spends 2 bits per character (200 bits); Huffman spends 130.

Example

Input: frequencies = a: 70, b: 20, c: 10
Output: a → 1, b → 01, c → 00 (130 bits total)

Greedy idea

The most frequent character must have the shortest code — so build the tree from the rarest characters upward, merging the two least frequent nodes at every step.

Prefix requirement

For decompression to be unambiguous, no code may be a prefix of another. With a = 1, b = 01, c = 00 the stream 1 00 1 01 can only mean acab. Leaves of a binary tree automatically satisfy this.

High-level idea. Build a binary tree in which every input character is a leaf and internal nodes carry a dummy character ($). Label every left edge 0 and every right edge 1; the root-to-leaf path spells out the leaf's code. Then traverse the tree and print the codes.

1
Create the leaves
One node per character with its frequency; push all of them into a min-heap keyed on frequency.
2
Merge while the heap has more than one node
left = extractMin(), right = extractMin(); create a node with character $, frequency left.freq + right.freq, and the two popped nodes as children; push it back.
3
The last node is the root
Its frequency is the total character count.
4
Print the codes
printCodes(root, ""): at a leaf print the character and the accumulated string; otherwise recurse left with code + "0" and right with code + "1".
Ties

Two nodes may have the same frequency, and then the shape of the tree depends on which one the heap returns first. The code lengths — and the total compressed size — are identical either way, but the actual bit strings differ. The programs below break ties by insertion order so that all four print the same codes.

Time O(k log k) for k distinct characters (k − 1 merges, each O(log k) on the heap)Space O(k) for the tree
Pitfall

A text with a single distinct character produces a tree that is just one leaf and an empty code "". Real encoders special-case this (give it the code 0). Also remember that the frequency table must be stored alongside the compressed data, or the decoder cannot rebuild the same tree.

Interview Q&A

Greedy vs dynamic programming — how do you decide?

Both need optimal substructure. Greedy additionally needs the greedy-choice property: a locally best choice that is provably part of an optimal solution, so you never have to look at alternatives. DP is for problems where the best choice at a step depends on the solutions of sub-problems, so you must evaluate all options and keep the best (0/1 knapsack, general coin change, LCS). Greedy is faster — usually O(n log n) — but only when it is correct.

Why does greedy work for Indian/US coins but not for arbitrary denominations?

In canonical coin systems every coin is worth at least as much as any combination of smaller coins that it could replace, so taking the largest coin never costs an extra coin later. Arbitrary systems like {18, 10, 1} break that: 20 = 10 + 10 beats 18 + 1 + 1. Minimum coins for arbitrary denominations is a DP problem.

Sketch the exchange argument for activity selection.

Let g be the activity with the earliest finish and S an optimal solution whose first activity (by finish) is x ≠ g. Since g finishes no later than x, S − {x} + {g} has no overlaps and the same size — so there is an optimal solution containing g. Remove g and all activities overlapping it; the remainder is the same problem on fewer activities, so induction finishes the proof.

Why are Huffman codes prefix-free, and why does that matter?

Every character sits at a leaf of the tree, and a leaf's path can never be the prefix of another leaf's path (that other leaf would have to be inside its subtree). Prefix-freeness means the decoder can read bits one at a time and stop the moment it reaches a leaf — no separators between codes are needed.

Is Huffman coding optimal?

Yes — among all prefix codes for a given set of per-symbol frequencies it minimises the expected code length (proved by an exchange argument: in an optimal tree the two rarest symbols are sibling leaves at maximum depth). It is not optimal when symbols are correlated or when fractional bits per symbol would help — arithmetic coding and context modelling do better there.

Name a problem where the obvious greedy rule is wrong and give the counterexample.

0/1 knapsack by value-per-weight: W = 50, items (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120). Ratios pick items 1 and 2 for value 160, but items 2 and 3 give 220. Another: activity selection by shortest duration — a short activity in the middle can block two longer ones on either side.
